question: Driven by international tech corporations and private operators, the proliferation of data centres and digital infrastructure in Sicily could result in the island being exploited in order to benefit the digital sector and make money for Big Tech.

Compounding the issue is the fact that these facilities use a great deal of energy, water and land in a region that is bedevilled by inadequate infrastructure and social inequalities and is frequently gripped by critical water shortages.
No stranger to actors who plunder its resources without providing commensurate social benefits to local residents, Sicily could end up in the thrall of digital and energy colonialism.

A particular concern is that these new colonialists could power their extremely energyintensive facilities by using locally produced renewables that were meant to drive efforts to decarbonise Sicily’s public services, households and productive sector. I therefore ask the Commission: 1.

Does it hold that concentrating large data centres on an island that struggles with water and energy security to be compatible with the objectives of the Green Deal and the EU’s territorial cohesion policies?
What instruments will it leverage to prevent peripheral areas like Sicily from being exploited as energy and digital hubs by giant global operators?

What steps will it take to strengthen European digital sovereignty by ensuring that the establishment of new strategic infrastructure in the Mediterranean does not entrench the power of non-European Big Tech companies?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) Data centres are vital infrastructures for the competitiveness of the EU, as they power AI and cloud computing services. New technologies for data centres can minimise their environmental impacts and generate benefits for the regions hosting them.

The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act articulates1 a consolidated vision for cuttingedge cloud and AI technologies, including sustainable data centre technologies, and harmonises the conditions for investment in data centres across the EU, with a focus on highly sustainable and innovative data centres and data centres supporting essential public sector functions.

The Commission is working on a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package that will build on the solutions provided for in the Energy Efficiency Directive2 by introducing a rating scheme3 for the energy efficiency of data centres. The Commission will also launch a public consultation for possible minimum performance standards for data centres. The Cloud and AI Development Act also leverages several instruments.

It supports the deployment of sustainable data centres meeting high standards of energy and water efficiency, as well as contributing to grid stability, but it does not substitute national, regional or local decisions when it comes to permitting procedures.

It supports national and regional authorities in conditioning project approvals, on clear local benefits, and enables the Commission and local authorities to detect and correct imbalances early through enhanced monitoring.

Finally, the Cloud and AI Development Act also includes measures to ensure equitable and non-discriminatory access to the essential resources underpinning data centre deployment across Europe, to avoid hoarding practices by some operators.
